items.title: Tim Willits doesn't think Rideshare's generative AI is damaging Saber's reputation
items.author: Julian Benson
items.summary: A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z,
items.text:
A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z, the company was dealing with the shitstorm that ensued from their announcement of Rideshare Stimulator.

The game's basically an Uber simulator, with you driving a car around town picking up fares, but Saber drew all kinds of bad attention when a former writer on the game revealed the game featured generative AI (something left undisclosed on the game's Steam page until recently) and CEO Matt Karch responded by attacking the writer in statements to the press. Something he has since apologised for.

So, naturally, we talked about generative AI and the reputational damage – or lack of – when getting caught out using it.

Watch on YouTube

Rideshare will have a main narrative, similar to other simulator games, in which you start your business in a city and grow it up as you complete jobs. Similar to something you would play through in Snowrunner. "All that is written by humans, all the missions are written by humans," Willits tells me. Where the generative AI appears is in Rideshare's Free Ride mode.

In Free Ride, when you pick up a fare, their dialogue will be generated using an LLM. "What we want to do is feed current events, like maybe there's some soccer game, and some ride will get in and talk about it," Willits explains. He says Saber are "using it here in a small part of a small game to test the waters." and that the company are "interested in how AI can help in games."

Willits says Rideshare is the only game in which Saber are using generative AI – "We don't have AI in Space Marine. We don't have AI in Hellraiser. We don't have AI in Jurassic Park, but we want to figure it out and we want to try something."

When I spoke with Willits, the thing I most wanted to know was why there was no AI disclosure on the Rideshare's Steam page when it was first revealed. Valve have a clear policy on disclosing the use of generative AI both in the production of a game and if any feature of the game makes ongoing calls to LLMs.

The reason, Willits says, is they "had an announce plan, but that got a little sideways". There was going to be a sneak peak, then there would have been reveals of the game's features in the future, and as part of that the generative technology would have been revealed. To indicate how early in the game's reveal rollout they are, Willits points out Rideshare's "not here" at Gamescom. "Unfortunately, we had some people talk about the game when they weren't supposed to be talking about the game and that just kind of escalated."

Though, I bring it back to Valve's AI disclosure policy because it doesn't make a distinction between whether a feature has been announced or not, only whether the technology is used in a game. Shouldn't the disclosure still have been there when the game was announced? "Okay, sure," Willits says.

The point I'm building to with Willits is that by not initially disclosing the use of AI, it seeds doubt about generative AI's use in Saber's other games. The tool may have been used but the company is not yet ready to announce or reveal it. I point to another of Saber's games, Road Kings, a new American trucking simulator which I really enjoyed at a preview event in April. While on the road, other drivers or job brokers may message you to ask for help, spurring an emergent quest. Certainly, there's no suggestion that these quests are generated by AI, but to a player the two systems could appear similar and they may now question 'Is this generative AI Saber's not copped to yet?'. "You may be overthinking it a little bit," Willits says. "I wouldn't worry about that. Again, the wishlists are up, interest is up, preorders across our games are up."

I didn't want to move on immediately, as Road Kings captures the issue well. I saw the game back in April but its embargo for the preview only came up after the Rideshare story had broken. I played and enjoyed that game and its mix of American Truck Simulator-style hauling blended with scenes you might see in a disaster move like Twister. But the comments on the preview were largely about the Rideshare news and Saber's use of AI. Willits, again, disagrees this is an issue. "I wouldn't really worry about that," he says. "The games will speak for themselves. You enjoyed Road Kings. The people that play it, they will enjoy it. I've been in the industry for 30 whatever years, you will always get crazy comments."

Willits points back to when he was working at id and they announced Quake 3 would need a video card to play. "We were roasted," he says. "The internet hate was crazy. 'You're ruining the industry. How can you make me pay $100 for a video card?' – imagine a $100 video card! – But the game came out and people liked it."

Willits also points to the launch of Steam, which, while a well-regarded platform now, was not universally loved at launch. In part because its servers struggled and its online functionality demanded more from peoples' internet than a lot of dial up and early broadband connections could provide. "I think we're in a period now of technology change that people are really unsure about," Willits says. "We, as game developers, don't really know what we're doing with it yet. Players don't really know what's going on with it. But I do think that there will be a game from somebody that will be so awesome that everyone will be like 'That's it. Now I get it.' I think the games will speak for themselves and when people play or they read your stories, and they watch the videos and they see the content, they will make their own determination."

As I've said in the past to other developers, I can believe there are ways these new AI technologies could benefit my work. For instance, the first transcription pass of most my interviews is done automatically because I use Google's Recorder app. But I also know the worst thing I could do with [insert AI tool of your choice] would be to generate an article for RPS. No one comes to this site to see something cobbled together by an LLM, they want something lovingly stitched together by these dyslexic typo-spewing hands. So I ask Willits what he thinks the benefit for Saber will be.

"As a game developer, if you're going to try something with brand new generative AI, it's much better to try it with something small [rather] than your biggest title," Willits says. "For us, part of our strategy at Saber is to make our mega hits – Space Marine 3, Jurassic Park, Turok – but we have to have smaller games that are consistent when it comes to how long it takes to make, how much money they make, [that's where] we experiment with things. Look at Spintires. That was an experiment that turned into a mega franchise. Rideshare fits into that category. It is a Rideshare simulator, where you drive around and you pick people up. There's really not much more you can really do there. And so for us, we wanted to be like 'Well, let's try this. Let's try it here because if it doesn't work out, it's on that game. It's not on our mega hits.'"

In the case of Rideshare's Free Ride mode, Willits says "This is a gameplay feature that is not possible without this technology. It would be logistically too hard, it'd be so expensive. We'd have to have an army." And, as he's described it, a mode where passenger dialogue is generated in response to current events fed into the game, I agree. Either you would have a madlibs style system of words being swapped in and out of repeating schemas, or a human writer adding additional lines in response to real world news events.

I do want to see if Saber are able to produce anything better than the other games that have stuck LLMs inside the throats of their characters. In Where Winds Meet, players quickly convinced one of the NPCs that they were pregnant, and another to provide cooking advice for potatoes and ketchup. That implementation and others were panned by developers Samuel Horti spoke to back in December.

My experience of generative AI dialogue has largely been formulaic and predictable. Which, could make for incredibly dreary car journeys. Ironically, the last taxi ride I was in I told the driver he was taking us to an engagement meal and he told me how AI was going to destroy the world by 2030.

Travel and accommodation to Gamescom was provided by the conference organisers.

items.title: "We track every server you enter": the Wardogs devs are "coming down hard" on XP farms and cash exploits, even as they encourage people to grind
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: The creators of military shooter Wardogs have announced that they will crack down heavily on players who use exploits and bugs to speedily farm in-game
items.text:
The creators of military shooter Wardogs have announced that they will crack down heavily on players who use exploits and bugs to speedily farm in-game currency and XP, or who spend “more than a few minutes” in servers created for this purpose.

Given that Wardogs advertises itself as a shooter about getting rich – a game in which "cash is king", with individualised payouts for a bunch of different in-game actions - I do feel like Bulkhead are sending mixed messages, even by the standards of incoherent wargames. Trying to define 'fairly earned' in a game that encourages you to be a frenzied, gun-toting plutomaniac is surely plunging headfirst into farce. Mind you, I respect the desire to Maintain The Fun for players who aren't quite as dollar-driven, and avoid having a community browser slammed with servers called "[EU/DOGF$RM]" or similar.

Wardogs launched in early access last week, reaching an audience of over 400,000 simultaneous Steam players by Sunday. James spent some time in it last week, and returned with many thrilling gigwork anecdotes. The devs have now rolled out a patch aimed at improving the game's server browser, with a new dedicated feed for community servers.

"Community Servers are the lifeblood of FPS games like ours," they write on Steam. "We want to make sure we actively create technology in and out of the game that supports the growth and fostering of communities. We have failed to do that by rushing our Community Server strategy. As we've always said, when we're wrong, we'll hold our hands up. We got this bit wrong." In addition to the update, the devs are giving players in community servers an additional 5% End of Match cash bonus by way of apology. "So if you're looking to grind, we suggest jumping in a community server."

Steam Makes 10/10 Open-World Masterpiece Completely Free Until September 21

Published Sep 18, 2026, 5:37 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

The weekend is almost here once again, and after a long and arduous week, what better way to relax than by jumping into a highly rated game without having to spend a single penny?

Well, that is now possible for Steam users, as the PC storefront has made one of the most successful games of all time, completely free to download until 21 September, with absolutely no catch.

The game in question is none other than Sea of Thieves: 2026 Edition. First released back in 2020, the smash-hit pirate adventure game offers the quintessential pirate experience, tasking players with plundering lost treasures, partaking in intense naval battles, vanquishing sea monsters and more. Best yet, it can be enjoyed with friends.

The original game, Sea of Thieves, launched back in 2018, and since then, it has become one of the most successful multiplayer games of all time. However, that was not always the case. As one of the earliest first-party games to launch for Xbox Game Pass subscribers, initial reviews were mixed, with complaints over its progression and lack of content.

However, over the past few years, its developers, Rare, have put the work in, offering countless updates and content drops, and now, with the game being available on multiple platforms, its popularity has only grown.

So much so, that in June 2026, it was announced that a Sea of Thieves live-action movie was reportedly in development with Destin Daniel Cretton producing. It remains to be seen if this ever comes to fruition, but it is an exciting prospect nonetheless.

In the meantime, however, PC users can now get their hands on Sea of Thieves: 2026 Edition on Steam for absolutely free, with the 2026 Edition offering both the base game as well as all of its digital bonus media.

Sea of Thieves offers the essential pirate experience, from sailing and fighting to exploring and looting – everything you need to live the pirate life and become a legend in your own right. With no set roles, you have complete freedom to approach the world, and other players, however you choose.

Available to play solo or with friends, Sea of Thieves has earned its high rating, as players navigate a vast open-world, enjoy new seasonal content, and most importantly, become a legend of the sea.

On your journey to become a Pirate Legend you’ll amass loot, build a reputation and define a unique personal style with your hard-earned rewards. Adventurer. Explorer. Conqueror. What will your legend be?

Sitting at a 'Very Positive' rating on Steam, Sea of Thieves: 2026 Edition is not one to pass up on, and now, until 21 September, you can become a pirate for absolutely free simply by downloading the game and getting stuck in. So, what are you waiting for?

Zack Snyder Gives an Official Verdict on New Crime Thriller Following Negative Reviews

Warner Bros./courtesy Everett Collection

Director Zack Snyder is no stranger to fan support — his admirers rallied together and got Warner Bros. to fund a director's cut of Snyder's Justice League — but he created a monster, and the monster seems to have gotten out of control. Snyder's latest film, The Last Photograph, received venomous reviews after its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival, with many describing it as the worst film of the director's career and among the worst to have played at TIFF. Now, Snyder has reacted to the film's reception and made it clear that some of the allegations hurled at him, that he is a homophobe and a fascist, are entirely untrue.

In an interview with Variety, Snyder said that he was initially taken aback by the reactions, but a part of him feels that drawing such an extreme response from his audience is necessary. "The amount of energy and the amount of vitriol I find really incredible. 'I want to kill Zack Snyder.' 'Zack Snyder is a fascist.' 'Zack Snyder is a homophobe.' 'Zack Snyder is a bisexual'," he said, adding that he is obviously not a fascist. Snyder's last two features, the mega-budget Netflix sci-fantasy epics Rebel Moon – Part One: A Child of Fire and Rebel Moon – Part Two: The Scargiver, dealt with themes of fascism quite overtly. They were also critically panned, like The Last Photograph.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Personality Quiz
Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like?
Paul Atreides · Captain Kirk · Princess Leia · Ellen Ripley · Max Rockatansky

Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🏜️Paul Atreides

🖖Capt. Kirk

✊Princess Leia

🔦Ellen Ripley

🔥Max Rockatansky

FIND YOUR HERO →

01

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?
The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you.

AI absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward.
BI read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes.
CI rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction.
DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.
EI don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?
The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails.

APrescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly.
BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.
CConviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire.
DComposure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury.
EEndurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for?
Your deepest motivation is your truest compass.

AThe survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it.
BThe safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind.
CFreedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire.
DThe truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not.
EThe one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you relate to the people around you?
Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

AWith intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated.
BWith warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself.
CWith directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it.
DWith professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family.
EWith wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do?
How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything.

APrepare in silence. If they won't listen, I'll be ready when they finally have to.
BKeep pushing until someone listens — and if no one does, handle it myself.
CBuild the case, find the allies, and make the threat impossible to ignore.
DDocument everything. The truth matters even if no one believes it yet.
EStop trying to convince anyone. Survive it. That's the only argument that counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

What has your heroism cost you personally?
Every hero pays. The question is what — and whether they'd pay it again.

AMy innocence — I've seen what I'm capable of, and I can't unsee it.
BPeople I loved — the command chair has a view, but it's a lonely one.
CA normal life — I gave up everything ordinary the moment I chose the cause.
DMy sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise.
EAlmost everything — and I'm still not sure what I'm carrying it all for. But I keep going.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

How do you feel about the rules of the world you're in?
Every hero has a relationship with the system. What's yours?

AI understand them deeply — and I know exactly which ones must be broken, and why.
BI respect the spirit of them and bend the letter when the situation demands it.
CThe system is the problem. I'm not here to work within it — I'm here to dismantle it.
DI follow protocol until protocol stops being useful. Then I make the call myself.
EThe rules collapsed a long time ago. What's left is instinct, and mine are reliable.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

When everything is on the line, what keeps you going?
The answer is the most honest thing about you.

ADestiny — or something that feels so much like it that the difference no longer matters.
BThe people on my ship — their faces, their trust, the fact that they're counting on me.
CThe belief that what we're fighting for is worth every sacrifice, including this one.
DSheer refusal to let it win — whatever it is. I don't stop. That's just who I am.
EI'm not sure anymore. But the road is still there, and I'm still on it.

REVEAL MY HERO →

Your Hero Has Been Identified
Your Sci-Fi Hero Is…

Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.

Arrakis · Dune

Paul Atreides

You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.

You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you.

You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape.

Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway.

That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you.

USS Enterprise · Star Trek

Captain Kirk

You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.

You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously.

Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it.

Kirk's genius isn't tactical — it's human. He reads people, bends rules with purpose, and wills outcomes into existence through sheer conviction.

That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours.

The Rebellion · Star Wars

Princess Leia

You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.

You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable.

You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back.

Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.

That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.

The Nostromo · Alien

Ellen Ripley

You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.

You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.

Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.

You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.

When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.

The Wasteland · Mad Max

Max Rockatansky

You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.

You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.

Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.

Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.

That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

It currently holds a 21% score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, which is higher than both Rebel Moon movies. Snyder implied that the online backlash may be overblown. "There were only 1,200 people in the theater and there are thousands of comments," he said, adding, "Whether you like the movie or not, I’m not even commenting on that; but with me, it’s more clickable to say, 'I hate Zack Snyder! Published Sep 18, 2026, 1:30 AM EDT

Nicholas Becher is a gaming journalist with an MFA in Creative Writing from FAU. With extensive experience playing video games, he covers all forms of gaming content at Screen Rant, from breaking news to the latest fan theories. Most-played games range from Clair Obscur to Civ to Elden Ring to Halo 2 and beyond.

Dungeon Crawler Carl has gone from a relatively niche LitRPG series to one of the genre's most surprising success stories in just a few short years. Matt Dinniman's chaotic adventures of Carl and Princess Donut have exploded in popularity through both the novels and Jeff Hays' acclaimed audiobooks, with the eighth installment, A Parade of Horribles, becoming an instant #1 New York Times bestseller following its May 2026 release.

The mainline story is now approaching its end, with Dinniman working on Book 9, currently carrying the working title The Beautiful Place, which is expected to conclude the series across two physical volumes. However, the Dungeon Crawler Carl is poised to expand into a full-blown juggernaut IP spanning various mediums in the coming years.

One of its biggest expansions yet arrives later this year with the official Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG, giving fans the chance to enter the World Dungeon themselves and marking the official next major release for the franchise this November (via RGS).

Credit: Dandy House

Dungeon Crawler Carl's official tabletop RPG generated more than $13 million through its record-breaking crowdfunding campaign, proving just how popular the franchise has become lately. Those backers should be among the first players to enter the World Dungeon, as Renegade Game Studios has said physical crowdfunding fulfillment is scheduled to begin in October 2026, although the enormous number of orders means fulfillment is expected to take roughly six to eight weeks rather than arriving for everyone simultaneously.

The campaign previously targeted October delivery, with Renegade saying it hoped backers would be playing by Thanksgiving. That said, digital copies of the RPG materials have already begun going out to eligible backers ahead of physical fulfillment.

Everyone else will not have much longer to wait beyond that, fortunately. Renegade currently lists the Dungeon Crawler Carl Roleplaying Game and its related products for a November 2026 retail release, with the company previously specifying that the wider retail launch is planned for late November. The Core Rulebook and Starter Set are also available to preorder, alongside accessories including miniatures, dice, a GM screen, and more.

Ace Books

The RPG itself is a skill-based tabletop system designed to recreate the books' deadly televised World Dungeon. Players can step into the roles of established characters such as Carl, Princess Donut, Florin, and Prepotente, or create an original crawler using dozens of races, classes, backgrounds, and skills.

Campaigns incorporate familiar Dungeon Crawler Carl concepts including achievements, viewers and followers, loot boxes, crafting, bosses, rival crawlers, gods, factions, and the ever-present System AI. Renegade is already planning continued support through expansions and a digital Season Pass running from November 2026 through October 2027.

The crowdfunding campaign also covered Dungeon Crawler Carl: Unstoppable, a separate solo or two-player cooperative card-crafting game designed by John D. Clair. Players initially control Carl or Donut, physically upgrading sleeved cards as they battle through the dungeon.

The base game covers the first three floors, while the Iron Tangle expansion adds the Fourth Floor and Crawler Chaos introduces additional playable characters. Like the RPG, Unstoppable is currently scheduled for retail in November 2026, giving Dungeon Crawler Carl fans a lot to look forward to this Fall.

Published Sep 18, 2026, 1:00 AM EDT

Dhruv is a Lead Writer in Screen Rant's New TV division. He has been consistently contributing to the website for over two years and has written thousands of articles covering streaming trends, movie/TV analysis, and pop culture breakdowns.
Before Screen Rant, he was a Senior Writer for The Cinemaholic, covering everything from anime to television, from reality TV to movies.
After high school, he was on his way to become a Civil Engineer. However, he soon realized that writing was his true calling. As a result, he took a leap and never looked back.

David Fincher and William Gibson have long-established themselves as visionaries in their respective genres. While Fincher never fails to deliver some of the most compelling and psychologically dense thrillers, William Gibson's literary sci-fi legacy continues to influence new additions to the genre. One show seemingly draws from the works of both creatives and delivers an unforgettable 4-season story.

Created by Sam Esmail, Mr. Robot premiered in 2015 on the USA Network. Unlike most sci-fi thrillers that take their time to find their feet, Mr. Robot immerses viewers in its bleak yet fascinating New York City visuals and techno-drama from the very first episode. Despite delivering a top-notch pilot, the show refuses to slow down and only keeps raising the bar of its storytelling as it progresses.

Mr. Robot has one of the most realistic portrayals of hacking on the screen.

The series is further elevated by the incredible performances of its cast members and the brilliantly written characters they portray. While Mr. Robot never became a mainstream viral sensation, the show still has an unmatched cult following. Even its finale easily ranks among TV's greats.

Mr. Robot is a completely original series, but it is hard not to see how it works so well because it echoes David Fincher's movies and William Gibson's sci-fi books in more ways than one.

David Fincher’s Psychological Twists Meet William Gibson’s Post-Cyberpunk Vision In Mr. Robot

Almost like David Fincher's Fight Club, Sam Esmail's Mr. Robot introduces viewers to an unreliable narrator, Elliot (played by Rami Malek). Instead of knowing what is happening in the objective world, viewers are thrown into Elliot's subjective and often fractured perception of reality.

Similar to Fincher's Se7en and The Game, Mr. Robot also has this constant brooding atmosphere that hints at the existence of an omnipresent and invincible villain. Aligning with many Fincher movies, like The Killer, Fight Club, and The Social Network, Mr. Robot also raises questions and criticizes everything from the capitalist systems that control our lives to the ways technology influences human behavior.

Even from a visual standpoint, the show masterfully captures its protagonist's alienation and nihilism in a comforting yet chilling way. This reminds one of Fincher's distinct visual language.

While it is arguable whether Mr. Robot qualifies as a cybepunk series, it does adopt many tropes and devices from the sci-fi subgenre. It captures a world with clear class divides where E Corp ("Evil Corp") is essentially William Gibson’s Zaibatsu. The mega-conglomerate in the show is so sprawling that it even reigns above the national government.

Meanwhile, the show's protagonist, Elliot, is a "low-life" in a "high-tech" world, with hacking as the only weapon at his disposal. Elliot comes off as a console cowboy like Case from Gibson's Neuromancer, although he seems even more isolated and withdrawn than the iconic cyberpunk character.

Mr. Robot Has One Of The Best Pilots & Finales Of All Time

It is rare for a show to snag a viewer's attention in the first ten minutes without being overly flashy or dramatic. Mr. Robot, however, stands as an exception as it takes minutes to pull viewers into Elliot's paranoia and genius hacking abilities. Even the overarching infrastructure and main players of its post-cyberpunk story are established in the first episode itself.

Many sci-fi thrillers begin on a strong note and do a commendable job of presenting their ambitious ideas in their opening arcs. However, as they progress into their second and third seasons, they gradually lose steam and lose sight of their own vision. Mr. Robot remains top-notch throughout its runtime and rarely delivers any dull episodes.

Its finale, too, feels complete as it resolves every underlying story thread while completely reframing the beginning. Mr. Robot also has an incredibly high rewatch value, making it the perfect series for fans of David Fincher's psychological thrillers and William Gibson's sci-fi novels.

Young computer programmer Elliot struggles with drug abuse, an anti-social disorder, and paranoia, and connects to people by hacking them. When he is approached by a mysterious anarchist calling himself Mr. Robot, he joins a team of hacktivists called fsociety determined to take down the world's biggest corporations.

items.text:
There exists in classed-based military shooters an understanding: Never count on a random medic to care about you.

You'd think in games where players have to opt into the support role, it'd be as simple as "There's a medic nearby, they'll try to get me," but any Battlefield player will tell you how often trained doctors trample over their corpse, more hungry to end a life than save one. So you learn to assume that you're on your own, and when a real medic does go out of their way to help you, they're the exception that proves the rule.

Wardogs is different. Help is so abundant in this 100-player, three-team milsim that, when I die, I can be confident a second, third, or even a fourth chance is coming. It's the only FPS I've played where multiple medics will actually race to give me first-aid, drag my body to safety, or pop a smoke grenade to cover a revive.

I've also played shooters where support play is taken more seriously than in Battlefield—Squad, Hell Let Loose, Isonzo, Arma, and other games on the "milsim" spectrum come to mind—but Bulkhead has successfully crafted a medic role so accessible and appealing that damn near everyone in Wardogs wants to help. Official stats from Wardogs' first weekend reveal that players earned 123 million kills and 61 million revives for an overall resurrection rate of nearly 50%. As a lifelong medic main, that's astounding.

How does Wardogs do it? I think a lot of factors contribute:

(Image credit: Bulkhead)Money, obviously

The big one is Wardogs' unique, cash-infused incentive structure. Unlike an extraction shooter, where money is earned primarily through kills and selling valuable loot, Wardogs will make you rich just for doing useful, nonviolent things for the team: killing, capturing, transporting, spotting, building, and healing.

On top of the fuzzy feelings I get for helping out, Medic is a very profitable playstyle in Wardogs. A single revive pays almost as much as a kill, and that's before you factor in tips from grateful patients and automatic assist payouts when those patients go on to get more kills. If I go the extra mile of buying spare bandages to heal folks back to 100, I get even more cash and tips.

Battlefield 6 also showers dedicated medics with XP, and really good ones end up near the top of the scoreboard, but Wardogs' cash prizes feel more impactful because it's the currency that fuels everything you do. Going on a 50k profit run in a single life can mean I've taken a big step toward unlocking an expensive upgrade, or it can mean that I get to splurge on my next loadout with a bigger backpack or vehicle. It's smart stuff.

(Image credit: Bulkhead)Anyone can revive

You don't have to invest in medic gear to lend a hand. Anyone can drag bodies and revive friendlies, and the vendor gives away a single-use quick-revive tool once per life. There's a world where this design choice could've been controversial in Wardogs, because if anyone can revive, what do you need proper medics for? But Bulkhead has threaded the needle perfectly by making manual "hand" revives—where your soldier literally rubs their hands together for ~20 seconds like they're charging defibrillators paddles—extremely slow.

Teammates can and will try to save you this way, but upgrading to proper defibrillators (unlocked at medic level 11) is a dramatic upgrade. A kitted-up medic can have a full squad back on its feet in the same time as a single hand revive. And even though there are no enforced classes in Wardogs, defibs are expensive and take up your one "specialist" tool slot that could hold an RPG or binoculars instead. This ensures that anyone can heal, but not everyone can be a proper medic.

(Image credit: Team17)It's not that dangerous to be a medic

I have found that going for a revive in Wardogs is not as risky as in similar games. Often (but not always) when I sprint toward a dead body out in the open, I'm able to drag them behind cover without drama.

I suspect this has to do with how spread out the action is in Wardogs: a three-team structure means there's no singular front where all of the death happens, which also means there's not a single pile of dead bodies that enemies are staring at, waiting for medics to make a move. No, most of my Wardogs skirmishes have been smaller in scale—confrontations with two or three clustered enemies or a showdown with a single sniper I can't even see.

It's a stark contrast to Battlefield 6, where some maps are so congested (and the time-to-kill so short) that the three seconds it takes to equip defibs and use them is enough for someone to sprint around a corner and shoot you in the face. Wardogs' pace is far better suited for support play.

(Image credit: Bulkhead)Bribing is fun, but not as important as I thought

The bribes help. As Sean highlighted last week the ability to bribe nearby medics up to $500 to pick you up can grease the wheels in desperate scenarios. For the first few days of Wardogs, I'd max out my bribe every time because it was cheaper than losing a whole loadout, but I've noticed lately that many players will attempt a revive regardless because, as we've covered, the base pay for a revive is incentive enough.

(Image credit: Bulkhead)Dead players don't give up, because dying costs time and money

Wardogs is unique in its commitment to death costing time. There are no Battlefield-like squad spawns, no rally points, and not even FOBs themselves are respawn beacons. There are only two ways to get back in the action: Use your team's one APC (a mobile respawn vehicle with a long cooldown after use) or hitch a ride for the 3km journey from HQ.

Both options are more expensive, and often significantly slower, than just waiting for a revive. I can't overemphasize how important that is, because it means that dead players choose to be patient and give medics a chance. There's nothing I hate more as a support player than folks giving up on me as I'm trying to stick my neck out for them, but so far in Wardogs, this has happened exactly once.

It's still really early days for Wardogs, and the game itself keeps changing as players unlock increasingly elaborate tools, but I'm impressed with how well its rules, scale, gadgets, and incentives coalesce around cooperation. The medic role might be the best example of that synergy in action.

items.author: Ash Parrish

items.text:
I have never felt more free than I do playing The Blood of Dawnwalker.

When you’re the kind of RPG player I am, there is no video-game sin more heinous than leaving a quest uncompleted. I so crave the satisfaction of being able to inbox-zero my long list of objectives that I often avoid the biggest RPGs because I know that I won’t be able to achieve this state within them—I’ll run out of either time or energy first. I know this is a me thing, that games don’t put the proverbial gun to my head and demand I finish everything. But there’s always a poisonous worry of “Will I get the good ending?” or “Am I gonna miss an important or fun narrative beat?” if I leave something behind.

Dawnwalker absolves me of that fear, leaving me free to pursue rabbit holes or the big, impactful events to my undead heart’s content. And that freedom, ironically, comes from some rather rigid restrictions. But honestly, they’re not rigid enough.

The Blood of Dawnwalker—and I can’t believe that I’ve been incorrectly calling it Blood of the Dawnwalker the entire time; Rebel Wolves, get your naming shit together—revolves around the idea that you, Coen of Laslea, a family man thrust into impossible circumstances, have 30 days to save your family from being sacrificed in a vampire blood ritual. Those 30 days are divided into day and night segments. By day you’re a normal man, but come nightfall you transform into a blood-craving vrakhir, and certain actions you take or quests you pursue will eat up those segments until your 30 days are spent.

I love how the game weaves Coen’s blood-drinking compulsion into the narrative. At night if he’s not at full health, every conversation with an NPC is a dice roll with the option to “give into the hunger” getting harder to ignore (and easier to select) the more damaged he is. Combat is an engaged, thoughtful affair. You’re not just mashing buttons and slashing foes; you have to read their moves and respond in kind. Even on “fair” difficulty, enemies hit hard, but if you carefully select abilities and upgrades as you build Coen, he can hit back just as hard. It is delightful to deploy his Artery Strike move and see the real big damage numbers flash across the screen.

But whoever told you this game was an action RPG, lied. It is a brilliantly disguised time management sim. As Coen traipses about his valley, helping villagers with their mundane problems, acquiring allies in his fight against the vampire overlords, or generally fucking up their operations, you can hear a subtle “click click click” reminding you that you’re on a clock. There’s even a visual representation; as you draw closer to a time-consuming task, the time-keeping bar in a corner of the screen flashes, indicating the blocks of time you’re gonna lose if you choose to pursue it.

It’s like a hot stove to my curious hand. Whenever I stumble upon a quest or activity, ready to do it just because it’s in front of me, I get pleasantly burned. Is the reward I’ll get for saving this random peasant on the road worth the time it’ll take for me to do it? Will I later regret not having more time to complete some other, more necessary task?

RPGs that let you do anything and everything have their place. But I think they’d be more compelling with the kind of restrictions Dawnwalker forces you to contend with. Developers understandably craft their games for the ease and comfort of players. Dawnwalker forces players into discomfort. No, you don’t get to do everything this time. You have to make a choice and then live with its consequences (more or less). That friction feels good. Embrace it.

Type of Game

Liked

With either combat or questing, there is no part of the game you can mindlessly plow through. The fantasy races in the game are some of the most unique I've ever seen. Some really cool romances including a very fun vampire sex scene.

Disliked

The time-restrictions are too permissive. Ho-hum "good" ending.

Platforms

PS5, Xbox Series S and X, Steam

Release Date

September 3rd

Played

Completed roughly every major objective in 34 hours.

The time system circumvents typical player psychology and makes you think harder and more deliberately about how you spend your time instead of letting you just mindlessly Robin Hood your way through a map. Now that I’ve been freed from the expectation of completion, Dawnwalker forces a presence of mind that I’ve rarely felt playing a sprawling RPG like this.

But I don’t think it goes far enough.

Just like I take issue with quests rooted in moral choice having a third, secret, make-everybody-happy solution, I think Dawnwalker’s permissiveness through restriction is slightly undermined by how much time you’re given to save your family.

In the game’s prologue—and my goodness what a prologue, Dawnwalker’s opening cinematic punched me through the chest and yanked hard—you’re introduced to the time-keeping mechanic by having Coen help out neighbors in his village. There’s a woman distressed because her grandson’s grave has been robbed, one guy’s missing his pig, and so on. You’re given the day to complete as many tasks as you can, but it’s impossible to do them all. Day turns to night and you run out of time. I’m haunted by the fact I never found out who destroyed that little boy’s grave, in favor of finding a lost pig. Womp womp.

That delicious pain, the kind that comes from having to make tough choices about what to do and what to leave undone, never really returns in the full game. In Dawnwalker there are several ways to build your power and unlock the final confrontation against the vampires holding your valley hostage in the 30 days you’re given. I was able to:

Get the most powerful legendary sword

Complete two romances and unlock a third

Obtain the most powerful armor

Kill all three vampire lieutenants

Obtain the highest infamy rating by disrupting vampire lieutenant operations and

Unlock access to all four main endings

All with four days left to spare.

To be clear, there are some things I missed, allies I didn’t make and stories I left unresolved. But I think the overall conceit of Dawnwalker would have hit so much harder if the time limit didn’t allow for so much. Shaving 10 or even five days off the 30-day time limit would have caused me some real pain and suffering as I would have been forced to make consequential, game-changing decisions. Think Mass Effect’s Kaidan vs. Ashley rather than synthesis, control, or destroy.

That said, The Blood of Dawnwalker is my GOTY 2026 frontrunner. The internal friction it inspires, playing against typical RPG conventions, makes it a must-play. I’m excited that Rebel Wolves has already announced it’s working on a sequel, and the game’s end-credits stinger hooked me just as hard as its opening cinematic. I just hope the sequel is meaner to its players. We don’t deserve comfort; it’s time to make us hurt.

items.title: Valheim devs finally get around to reading 5 years of player feedback, let you remap dodge key
items.author: clivingston@pcgamer.com (Christopher Livingston)
items.summary: When battling tree-swinging trolls, ice-spitting dragons, and fire-breathing skeletal demigods, it's hard to think of a skill more important than dodging. A
items.text:
When battling tree-swinging trolls, ice-spitting dragons, and fire-breathing skeletal demigods, it's hard to think of a skill more important than dodging. A shield or a weapon held up defensively can help, sure, but escaping deadly attacks in Valheim is often down to how quickly you can tuck and roll.

Which makes it a bit curious that over the past five years of early access, you couldn't redbind the dodge skill to a single key or button press. If you want to dodge on keyboard, you have to hold the block button (mouse 2) and press jump (space bar) and pick a direction (WASD). On controller, it's a stick + button combo. No single tap for a deeply important maneuver has been available for the past five years.

Until today! Those busy Valhiem devs finally took a peek at player feedback and noticed the request people have been making constantly for the past five years, seven months, 15 days, 17 hours, and 22 minutes: You have now been granted the ability to remap your dodge key to an alternate—no doubt single-tap—configuration.

Better late than never?

That's not the only key rebinding option that's been added. You can rebind items on the radial wheel and hotbar, too. A much newer request, to disable the intro cinematic (which only appeared with Valheim 1.0 last week), has also been granted. There are also some bug fixes, notably more tinkering with the Valheim cheat-flagging feature that was mislabeling some players and resources as cheats.

Have a look at the full patch notes below, and good luck trying to unlearn the muscle memory you've developed for dodging with three different keys over the past five years or so. One note: the patch, devs say, "will require a few days to get uploaded to all platforms." I've checked and it's live on PC now, however.

Quality of Life:

Added several new keybinding options to the keyboard (Alternate dodge key, hotbar rebinding (on top of 1-8), support for rebinding radial wheel, support for removing keybinds)

Added accessibility setting to be able to toggle blocking

Add toggle to Gameplay settings to skip the intro cinematic on startup

When attacking, the player’s rotation now also snaps towards the intended attack direction when the “attack towards look direction” option is enabled, not just when it’s disabled.

Swapped Motion Sensor and Sheath keybinds on gamepad, returning Sheath to its original keybind. Motion Sensor can now be activated with the alt-key + Sheath button instead.

Optimizations:

Improved GPU performance when tessellation is disabled by eliminating unnecessary GPU overhead in this case.

Heightmap shadows are now calculated more accurately and at a lower performance cost.

Optimized particle systems in the main menu to reduce overdraw.

Multiple GPU performance improvements on Switch 2.

Bugs & Issues:

PlayerBase effect on some build pieces has been increased to block enemies more

Fixed inaccuracies in stick input pre-processing that made it heavily weighted towards axis-aligned movement and 30% too slow diagonally.

Jotun puffs and Magecaps no longer respawn.

Fix for player characters sometimes mistakenly being marked as temporary cheaters, leading to items dropped by monsters they kill being incorrectly marked as having a cheated origin.

Cheated stackable items no longer stack with regular items, preventing uncheated stacks from being “corrupted” into a cheated state.

Persistent Events devcommand (“pevents”) is now actually behind the devcommands toggle and not available in the console by default.

Fixed errors when using the grappling hook’s secondary attack on creatures.

Fixed various issues with Ashlands water (VFX, water damage not stopping)

Fixed a bug where characters didn’t save correctly when manually pressing Save while playing on a server hosted by someone else.

Disabled biomedata caching, fixing a bug where the cache could end up in an invalid state, making it impossible to join remote servers.

Fixed Deep North battleaxes tool tier, can now cut all the trees.

Made placeable boulders persist, only placeable on the ground, break if the ground they’re standing on goes away, and give ground-level support.

Updated Ballista to make it accept all new trophies (All Deep North enemies + Bjorn + Vile)

Timberwood build pieces no longer incorrectly show up in earlier biome locations

Fixed various crashes/errors that could happen in rare circumstances

Fixed a bug where Helmet of the Protector was craftable directly via the Black Forge

Fixed a bug where terrain modifications by players or monsters could lead to performance and portal issues in multiplayer, such as performance and portaling issues, terrain seams, and terrain modifications becoming undone

Updated Deep North and Winding Tunnels music for better balance and to remove some clicks when looping.

Now plays the correct music in Mörkhalla.

Better mixing of location music in the Deep North.

Tweaked Seal and Baby Seal colliders to better match their bodies.

Fixed an issue where the “No time for snoozing” achievement could sometimes not be unlocked in multiplayer

Fixed an issue where The Homesteader and The Architect achievements could unlock repeatedly.

Nintendo Switch 2: The TV output no longer switches from 120 Hz to 60 Hz while the virtual keyboard is open or while in the home menu when using the balanced graphics preset and playing online multiplayer, which caused a black screen while entering and leaving these menus.

PlayStation®5: The TV output no longer switches from 120 Hz to 60 Hz while in the home menu when using the balanced graphics preset, which caused a black screen when entering and leaving this menu.

PlayStation®5: The “Stronger Together” achievement is now achievable.

Steam: Fixed a bug where Steam Cloud could get stuck in an invalid state if the game crashed while saving.

items.title: Epic boss Tim Sweeney says the EU's social media ban for under-13s 'would be terrible for the next generation of humanity'
items.author: andy.chalk@pcgamer.com (Andy Chalk)
items.summary: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney says the European Union's plan to restrict social media use by children, including a complete ban for anyone under the age of 13,
items.text:
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney says the European Union's plan to restrict social media use by children, including a complete ban for anyone under the age of 13, is "terrible for the next generation of humanity" because of the impact it will have on the growth of creativity and expression.

Announced today, the EU KIDS Act—"Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy," because overwrought acronyms for serious legislation isn't a uniquely American phenomenon—imposes a blanket ban on social media accounts for anyone under the age of 13, although "specially-designed child-friendly video-sharing services" can be established via their parents' or guardian's accounts.

From the ages of 13 to 15, accounts can be set up under the supervision of guardians, although they should have "limited features and screen time." From 15 up, minors can set up their own "autonomous accounts" without parental consent, although "parental guidance remains essential during this stage."

The goal of the new regulations is to effect a "gradual approach" to social media use—the digital equivalent of teaching kids to swim before throwing them into the lake. Notably, the KIDS Act covers not just traditional social media platforms—Instagram, TikTok, and the like—but also "video-sharing platforms, online games, AI chatbots or companions," plus app stores and operating systems. Some services, like online encyclopedias, educational platforms, and digital news outlets, would be exempt.

"Today, our children are engaging with the most sophisticated technologies ever created. Technology that was never created with their wellbeing in mind," EU president Ursula von der Leyen said in a statement. "Our KIDS Act is reversing the burden of proof—it is for platforms to show they are safe by design. And we put parents back in the driving seat, giving them the tools to help their children navigate a safer online world."

Sweeney takes a different view of the situation, however. "This would be terrible for the next generation of humanity," the Epic chief said on X, a day prior to the act's official announcement. "The apps and games of today are the paintbrushes and tree forts of yesterday. Fortnite has Creative Mode, Roblox has Roblox studio, and being a digital creator is in everyone's reach, till politicians take it away."

(Image credit: Tim Sweeney (Twitter))It's fair to say that it would not be great news for Epic if the EU suddenly made it a whole lot harder for kids under 15 to play Fortnite, and without wanting to sound like an 'in my day we drank straight from the hose!' guy, I would point out that paintbrushes and tree forts are still readily available. It's not as if pre-teens will be reduced to cave painting and hitting each other with rocks if they're suddenly no longer able to generate content for billionaires.

Even so, I find myself on board with Sweeney's broader stance—this isn't a great idea—not out of concerns that it will dull the creative instincts of the next generation, but simply because it's a potential security and privacy nightmare that's difficult to enforce and may or may not achieve its stated goals anyway.

And as other PC Gamer writers have previously pointed out, the impact of social media on young minds is only part of the problem, and arguably a relatively minor part: It also bakes the brains of adults with startling efficiency.

The EU KIDS Act is not a done deal. The proposed regulation has been submitted to the European Parliament and Council, and from there will enter the legislative process required for approval. Given the recent enactment of social media bans for kids and online age verification requirements in Australia, the UK, and some US states, though, and "the clear demand for urgent and comprehensive action" expressed by the EU, I expect it will be soon enough.

items.summary:
A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It’s Addictive

Unlike the pillowy-soft focaccia that’s more
items.text:
A Tiny Town in the Italian Riviera Has Its Own Version of Focaccia, and Let This Be a Warning—It’s Addictive

Unlike the pillowy-soft focaccia that’s more widely known, focaccia di Recco is thin, crispy and filled with gooey cheese

This summer, I found myself on a mission. As temperatures soared into the mid-90s during Europe’s heat wave, I packed my bags and embarked on a six-hour road trip from Switzerland to Liguria. Rather than seeking out seasonal treats like granita or gelato, I was headed to the Italian coast for focaccia.

When most Americans­—and Italians, for that matter—think of focaccia, they think of the pillowy-soft version that’s leavened with yeast, baked in a sheet pan and perfect for scarpetta, or the mopping up of delicious sauces. However, ask any Ligurian, and they will tell you that the focaccia that reigns supreme is focaccia di Recco.

Focaccia di Recco is a specialty dish in Liguria. Starkly different from the carbohydrate found in the United States, this yeast-free snack is a thin flatbread filled with gooey cheese—usually crescenza or stracchino—and baked in a super-hot oven until crispy and golden brown.

Certified as just one of four foods of the Ligurian coast with a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation from the European Union, an official focaccia di Recco can be made only in Recco or neighboring Camogli, Sori or Avegno. Along with sea-salt cured anchovies, basil and olive oil, focaccia di Recco is the pride of the Ligurian people. For two decades, a consortium, the Consorzio della Focaccia di Recco, has safeguarded the legend of the bread by promoting it through annual events like the Recco Focaccia Festival.

“The focaccia di Recco celebrates authenticity, local traditions and is a connection between food, people and place,” says Giovanni Astolfoni, a Genoa native who is executive chef of Botanico Restaurant in Nervi. “It is much more than a local specialty. It perfectly reflects the spirit of Ligurian cooking. … It looks simple, yet making it well takes experience, patience and respect for the ingredients.”

Even revered pizza makers in Italy hold focaccia di Recco in high esteem, agreeing that it is worth the pilgrimage. “What impresses me most is its simplicity and the incredible craftsmanship behind it,” says Francesco Capece, owner of Confine in Milan, recently named Italy’s best pizzeria. “With just a few ingredients, it creates a perfect balance between the crispy, paper-thin dough and the creamy cheese filling. It is a beautiful example of how Italian tradition transforms simple ingredients into something extraordinary.”

History of Focaccia di Recco

According to the consortium, the history of focaccia di Recco can be traced back to 1189, when a version of the bread appeared on the table of medieval knights before they made their departure for the Holy Land during the Third Crusade. However, it was during the raids by Saracen pirates around the 16th century that focaccia di Recco became what it is today, confirms Lucio Bernini, the consortium’s director. Research shows that as locals from Recco fled to the mountains, the ingredients they carried with them—flour, oil and cheese—were combined and cooked over slate stone. At the end of the 1800s, bakeries and taverns sold focaccia di Recco to residents in celebration of All Souls’ Day (November 2), the day after All Saints’ Day, which marks a two-day Christian observance of saints and martyrs, as well as those who are deceased. Nowadays, focaccia di Recco is a staple in the Ligurian diet, with locals in the region’s four provinces having constant access to it throughout the day.

Did you know? The earliest focaccia

Neolithic communities in the Middle East were baking focaccia-like flatbreads between 7000 and 5000 B.C.E., according a 2024 study in Scientific Reports.

In the 19th century, Panificio Moltedo, a bakery that still stands in Recco, was the first to sell focaccia di Recco. The now fifth-generation-owned bakery recently celebrated its 150th year making its wafer-thin pastry; unlike other bakeries and taverns, Panificio Moltedo does not bake its focaccia in a pan but rather directly on the deck of the oven, like a pizza, for maximum crispness. Another longtime favorite is Manuelina. The restaurant’s namesake ran a tavern outside of Recco in the late 1800s and is credited with making focaccia di Recco mainstream by serving it every day. Her descendants opened a simple focacceria in town in 1983 to keep up with demand. “Manuelina took the popular recipe and was the first to start selling it every day and for everyone to enjoy, But they did not invent focaccia di Recco,” says Bernini.

In the past century and a half, a handful of other eateries have opened along the Italian Riviera selling focaccia di Recco. One of those is Revello Camogli in the resort town of Camogli. “We have been making focaccia di Recco ever since my grandfather took over the business in 1964,” says third-generation owner Umberto Revello. “Running a bakery like ours requires a great deal of time, so the bakery becomes a second home—if not the first. Since we were children, we have grown up watching our father and grandfather make focaccia every day. It naturally became part of our family tradition.” He says that it’s more than a family business; focaccia represents an important part of his identity.

Second-generation focaccia di Recco maker Fabrizio Passano agrees. “My father, Alfredo, started making focaccia di Recco in 1967, and for the last 59 years, we have continued the tradition,” says the chef at Alfredo Ristorante in Recco. “Focaccia di Recco is a symbol of an ancient tradition we hold incredibly dear.”

Once I arrived in Recco, the focaccia, advertised on blackboard menus and in bakeries around town, was hard to miss. The blisters that formed on the roof of my mouth as I sampled different vendors’ versions of the bread filled with piping hot cheese were well worth it.

“While every restaurant has their own differences in technique, there really is only one recipe,” says Passano, acknowledging the focaccia’s PGI status. “So you have to stick with the plan.” When I stop into Alfredo Ristorante, the chef tosses the focaccia dough in the air with very little effort. Clearly, he has made many, and the result is a very thin and crispy focaccia. The cheese is chewy and makes a squeaking noise when I bite into it.

Over lunch at Alfredo, Bernini tells me the consortium consists of 12 members with 19 destinations, including bakeries, take-away eateries and restaurants spread across the Ligurian coast. “The PGI preserves the true history and tradition against increasingly widespread imitations,” the former hotelier adds.

According to Bernini, without the PGI stamp, the focaccia should not be called focaccia di Recco and should bear the name focaccia col formaggio (focaccia with cheese). A handful of restaurants in the United States, including Chi Spacca in Los Angeles, Rosie Cannonball in Houston and Keste in New York City, have the specialty on their menus.

How to make focaccia di Recco

According to Bernini, Passano and Revello, achieving a perfect focaccia di Recco comes down to the skills of the focacciai (a Ligurian term for focaccia makers). But all three agree that you can make the bread at home with a few simple tips.

“An important element to making a great focaccia di Recco is using high-quality ingredients,” says Revello. He continues, “Firstly, the flour. We use a strong Italian Type ‘0’ flour, which has an appearance of traditional white flour while retaining the most valuable parts of the wheat grain.”

The biggest difference between pizza dough and focaccia di Recco dough, Capece says, is that the latter contains no yeast. “It is made to be stretched extremely thin, while remaining elastic and strong enough to hold the cheese filling.”

And the cheese? Many bakers are steadfast in saying that only crescenza should be used. “We use only carefully selected crescenza cheese with a low fat content, otherwise, the cheese would melt too much during baking and would not give the desired result,” explains Revello.

Focaccia di Recco is typically baked in a pan, and this is where the true skill of a baker shines. “The dough must be stretched into an extremely thin sheet, almost transparent, and only experienced hands can achieve that consistency,” says Revello. “You should almost be able to see through the top layer before baking. This is one of the defining characteristics of an authentic focaccia di Recco.”

Baking the bread in a pizza oven is ideal. “Both pizza and focaccia di Recco require very high temperatures, but the goals are different,” says Capece. “Pizza needs a balanced heat from both the bottom and the top to develop a crisp base and a well-cooked crust. Focaccia di Recco also needs intense heat, but especially from above, to quickly brown the thin dough while keeping the cheese creamy.”

Revello adds that the main limitation of a home oven is its maximum temperature. “At lower temperatures, the focaccia needs to bake for longer, which tends to dry out the dough rather than keeping it light and delicate,” he says.

“Every focacciaio has a unique touch,” says Bernini. “That is why we invite all our guests to try various bakeries or restaurants of our consortium.”

Revello has tried many versions of focaccia di Recco, but, in his opinion, nothing beats “sitting on the beach, eating it with your hands while looking out at the sea in Camogli.”

Revello Camogli’s Focaccia di Recco Recipe

Ingredients

4 cups (500 grams) Type 0 flour (may substitute bread flour)

¼ cup (50 grams) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for the pan

1 cup (about 240 grams) water

1 teaspoon fine salt

Approximately 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram) of fresh crescenza (stracchino) cheese

Directions

To make the dough, mix the flour, oil, water and salt until well combined. Let the dough rest for about 30 minutes.

If you have a pizza oven, preheat it to 570°F. Otherwise, preheat a home oven to its maximum heat, about 500°F.

Divide the dough into two pieces, one about two-thirds of the total. Place the larger piece on a well-oiled pizza pan and stretch to cover the pan. Drop dots of cheese all over the dough. Roll or hand-stretch the smaller piece of dough as thinly as possible. Lay this thin sheet on top of the cheese. Prick large holes in the dough to let out any trapped air.

Bake the focaccia for 7 to 8 minutes, or longer if you’re baking at a lower heat. It is ready when the top is golden and the bottom slides freely on the baking pan. Slice and serve while hot.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/2Ht5uDMp7uS_kh4NdYKp4LgDvYs=/1026x684/filters:focal(1061x707:1062x708)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/94/b5/94b559ec-2e96-4ec2-b75f-599585cefacd/gettyimages-1475006586.jpg

This summer, I found myself on a mission. As temperatures soared into the mid-90s during Europe’s heat wave, I packed my bags and embarked on a six-hour road trip from Switzerland to Liguria. Rather than seeking out seasonal treats like granita or gelato, I was headed to the Italian coast for focaccia.

When most Americans­—and Italians, for that matter—think of focaccia, they think of the pillowy-soft version that’s leavened with yeast, baked in a sheet pan and perfect for scarpetta, or the mopping up of delicious sauces. However, ask any Ligurian, and they will tell you that the focaccia that reigns supreme is focaccia di Recco.

Focaccia di Recco is a specialty dish in Liguria. Starkly different from the carbohydrate found in the United States, this yeast-free snack is a thin flatbread filled with gooey cheese—usually crescenza or stracchino—and baked in a super-hot oven until crispy and golden brown.

Certified as just one of four foods of the Ligurian coast with a Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation from the European Union, an official focaccia di Recco can be made only in Recco or neighboring Camogli, Sori or Avegno. Along with sea-salt cured anchovies, basil and olive oil, focaccia di Recco is the pride of the Ligurian people. For two decades, a consortium, the Consorzio della Focaccia di Recco, has safeguarded the legend of the bread by promoting it through annual events like the Recco Focaccia Festival.

“The focaccia di Recco celebrates authenticity, local traditions and is a connection between food, people and place,” says Giovanni Astolfoni, a Genoa native who is executive chef of Botanico Restaurant in Nervi. “It is much more than a local specialty. It perfectly reflects the spirit of Ligurian cooking. … It looks simple, yet making it well takes experience, patience and respect for the ingredients.”

Even revered pizza makers in Italy hold focaccia di Recco in high esteem, agreeing that it is worth the pilgrimage. “What impresses me most is its simplicity and the incredible craftsmanship behind it,” says Francesco Capece, owner of Confine in Milan, recently named Italy’s best pizzeria. “With just a few ingredients, it creates a perfect balance between the crispy, paper-thin dough and the creamy cheese filling. It is a beautiful example of how Italian tradition transforms simple ingredients into something extraordinary.”

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/F24Ec8E4KLTE4x6gM8Hm9MuYNXE=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(1061x707:1062x708)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/09/b2/09b2daca-b1f6-4f67-ad72-f5445984d38f/gettyimages-2076422468.jpg
History of Focaccia di Recco

According to the consortium, the history of focaccia di Recco can be traced back to 1189, when a version of the bread appeared on the table of medieval knights before they made their departure for the Holy Land during the Third Crusade. However, it was during the raids by Saracen pirates around the 16th century that focaccia di Recco became what it is today, confirms Lucio Bernini, the consortium’s director. Research shows that as locals from Recco fled to the mountains, the ingredients they carried with them—flour, oil and cheese—were combined and cooked over slate stone. At the end of the 1800s, bakeries and taverns sold focaccia di Recco to residents in celebration of All Souls’ Day (November 2), the day after All Saints’ Day, which marks a two-day Christian observance of saints and martyrs, as well as those who are deceased. Nowadays, focaccia di Recco is a staple in the Ligurian diet, with locals in the region’s four provinces having constant access to it throughout the day.
Did you know? The earliest focaccia
Neolithic communities in the Middle East were baking focaccia-like flatbreads between 7000 and 5000 B.C.E., according a 2024 study in Scientific Reports.

In the 19th century, Panificio Moltedo, a bakery that still stands in Recco, was the first to sell focaccia di Recco. The now fifth-generation-owned bakery recently celebrated its 150th year making its wafer-thin pastry; unlike other bakeries and taverns, Panificio Moltedo does not bake its focaccia in a pan but rather directly on the deck of the oven, like a pizza, for maximum crispness. Another longtime favorite is Manuelina. The restaurant’s namesake ran a tavern outside of Recco in the late 1800s and is credited with making focaccia di Recco mainstream by serving it every day. Her descendants opened a simple focacceria in town in 1983 to keep up with demand. “Manuelina took the popular recipe and was the first to start selling it every day and for everyone to enjoy, But they did not invent focaccia di Recco,” says Bernini.

In the past century and a half, a handful of other eateries have opened along the Italian Riviera selling focaccia di Recco. One of those is Revello Camogli in the resort town of Camogli. “We have been making focaccia di Recco ever since my grandfather took over the business in 1964,” says third-generation owner Umberto Revello. “Running a bakery like ours requires a great deal of time, so the bakery becomes a second home—if not the first. Since we were children, we have grown up watching our father and grandfather make focaccia every day. It naturally became part of our family tradition.” He says that it’s more than a family business; focaccia represents an important part of his identity.

https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/k76zo0eHJpoLSlVRr60EmIQ0-78=/fit-in/1072x0/filters:focal(512x341:513x342)/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/filer_public/17/81/178181e4-d0ae-4925-bf85-5359eada25f2/gettyimages-1314659361.jpg
blocks.c: foccacia di Recco at Moltedo bakery

blocks.x: Second-generation focaccia di Recco maker Fabrizio Passano agrees. “My father, Alfredo, started making focaccia di Recco in 1967, and for the last 59 years, we have continued the tradition,” says the chef at Alfredo Ristorante in Recco. “Focaccia di Recco is a symbol of an ancient tradition we hold incredibly dear.”

Once I arrived in Recco, the focaccia, advertised on blackboard menus and in bakeries around town, was hard to miss. The blisters that formed on the roof of my mouth as I sampled different vendors’ versions of the bread filled with piping hot cheese were well worth it.

“While every restaurant has their own differences in technique, there really is only one recipe,” says Passano, acknowledging the focaccia’s PGI status. “So you have to stick with the plan.” When I stop into Alfredo Ristorante, the chef tosses the focaccia dough in the air with very little effort. Clearly, he has made many, and the result is a very thin and crispy focaccia. The cheese is chewy and makes a squeaking noise when I bite into it.

Over lunch at Alfredo, Bernini tells me the consortium consists of 12 members with 19 destinations, including bakeries, take-away eateries and restaurants spread across the Ligurian coast. “The PGI preserves the true history and tradition against increasingly widespread imitations,” the former hotelier adds.

According to Bernini, without the PGI stamp, the focaccia should not be called focaccia di Recco and should bear the name focaccia col formaggio (focaccia with cheese). A handful of restaurants in the United States, including Chi Spacca in Los Angeles, Rosie Cannonball in Houston and Keste in New York City, have the specialty on their menus.
How to make focaccia di Recco

According to Bernini, Passano and Revello, achieving a perfect focaccia di Recco comes down to the skills of the focacciai (a Ligurian term for focaccia makers). But all three agree that you can make the bread at home with a few simple tips.

“An important element to making a great focaccia di Recco is using high-quality ingredients,” says Revello. He continues, “Firstly, the flour. We use a strong Italian Type ‘0’ flour, which has an appearance of traditional white flour while retaining the most valuable parts of the wheat grain.”
https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/kiCDHCV08PtZ4CVonya7ng3cvh8=/fit-in/200x200/filters:no_upscale()/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/headshot/Michelle_Tchea-edit.png

The biggest difference between pizza dough and focaccia di Recco dough, Capece says, is that the latter contains no yeast. “It is made to be stretched extremely thin, while remaining elastic and strong enough to hold the cheese filling.”

And the cheese? Many bakers are steadfast in saying that only crescenza should be used. “We use only carefully selected crescenza cheese with a low fat content, otherwise, the cheese would melt too much during baking and would not give the desired result,” explains Revello.

Focaccia di Recco is typically baked in a pan, and this is where the true skill of a baker shines. “The dough must be stretched into an extremely thin sheet, almost transparent, and only experienced hands can achieve that consistency,” says Revello. “You should almost be able to see through the top layer before baking. This is one of the defining characteristics of an authentic focaccia di Recco.”

Baking the bread in a pizza oven is ideal. “Both pizza and focaccia di Recco require very high temperatures, but the goals are different,” says Capece. “Pizza needs a balanced heat from both the bottom and the top to develop a crisp base and a well-cooked crust. Focaccia di Recco also needs intense heat, but especially from above, to quickly brown the thin dough while keeping the cheese creamy.”

Revello adds that the main limitation of a home oven is its maximum temperature. “At lower temperatures, the focaccia needs to bake for longer, which tends to dry out the dough rather than keeping it light and delicate,” he says.
“Every focacciaio has a unique touch,” says Bernini. “That is why we invite all our guests to try various bakeries or restaurants of our consortium.”
Revello has tried many versions of focaccia di Recco, but, in his opinion, nothing beats “sitting on the beach, eating it with your hands while looking out at the sea in Camogli.”
Revello Camogli’s Focaccia di Recco Recipe
Ingredients
4 cups (500 grams) Type 0 flour (may substitute bread flour)
¼ cup (50 grams) extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for the pan
1 cup (about 240 grams) water
1 teaspoon fine salt
Approximately 2.2 pounds (1 kilogram) of fresh crescenza (stracchino) cheese
Directions
To make the dough, mix the flour, oil, water and salt until well combined. Let the dough rest for about 30 minutes.
If you have a pizza oven, preheat it to 570°F. Otherwise, preheat a home oven to its maximum heat, about 500°F.

Divide the dough into two pieces, one about two-thirds of the total. Place the larger piece on a well-oiled pizza pan and stretch to cover the pan. Drop dots of cheese all over the dough. Roll or hand-stretch the smaller piece of dough as thinly as possible. Lay this thin sheet on top of the cheese. Prick large holes in the dough to let out any trapped air.
Bake the focaccia for 7 to 8 minutes, or longer if you’re baking at a lower heat. It is ready when the top is golden and the bottom slides freely on the baking pan. Slice and serve while hot.
